passage: At the school canteen Arnab patted his empty pocket. "Lend me twenty, Gopika. We're best friends, aren't we?" It was the fifth time this month, and nothing from the earlier times had come back. Gopika's fingers curled around her coins. Her throat felt dry. What if he stopped sitting with her? "Not today," she said, very quietly. Arnab rolled his eyes. "Some best friend." Gopika ate her sandwich with hot cheeks, feeling both mean and used. That evening she told Mummy about it, and Mummy listened without interrupting and said they would think about it together.

qa.q: How many times had Arnab asked to borrow money this month?
qa.a: It was the fifth time this month.

qa.q: What was Gopika afraid of when Arnab asked again?
qa.a: She was afraid he would stop sitting with her if she said no, even though she felt used and mean at the same time.

qa.q: What could Gopika do if Arnab keeps asking?
qa.a: Politely refuse again and keep talking with a parent about it, as she began to do with Mummy.

qa.q: How might Arnab see the moment when Gopika said no?
qa.a: He may have been annoyed at hearing a no from someone who usually said yes; his "Some best friend" suggests he hoped friendship would make her agree.

grounding: Illustrates a child pressed by a friend who keeps borrowing money on the strength of friendship, feeling used but afraid to say so.

passage: I'm Maria. Last Saturday I had a hundred rupees saved for a sticker album, but at the toy stall I saw a tiny plush elephant and thought of my little sister Simran, who hugs everything she owns. Nobody had asked me to buy anything. I counted my coins twice. There was exactly enough for the elephant. When I gave it to her she pressed it against her cheek, shouted "Mine!" and ran to show Mummy. I had thought I would miss the sticker album. Strangely I didn't. My chest felt warm for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What did Maria buy for Simran?
qa.a: She bought a tiny plush elephant.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when Simran pressed the elephant against her cheek?
qa.a: A joy that was warmer than she expected, with no regret about the sticker album; her chest felt warm for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What could Maria remember about giving gifts to her sister?
qa.a: That the giving felt good because nobody pushed her, so she can say no when she does not want to give and give freely when she does 😊.

qa.q: How does Simran see the gift?
qa.a: She is delighted: she pressed it to her cheek, shouted "Mine!" and ran to show Mummy.

grounding: Illustrates a child freely spending her pocket money on a gift for her little sister and finding the giving joyful.

passage: I'm Samir, and I keep a small tin savings box under my bed. My father Francis and Mummy never count what's inside. They say it's mine to look after. That makes me feel trusted, and a bit heavy too. Last month I took ten rupees for a comic and forgot to write it in the little notebook. Nobody would have known. But at dinner I told Papa. He nodded. "Thank you for telling me. Write it down." He wasn't even cross. The box is still under my bed, and somehow it feels more mine than before.

qa.q: Where does Samir keep his savings?
qa.a: He keeps them in a small tin box under his bed.

qa.q: What was Samir worried about, and why did he tell his father anyway?
qa.a: He felt the trust was heavy and did not want to spoil it, so he told Papa about the comic even though nobody would have known.

qa.q: What would you advise Samir if he makes a bigger mistake with his money?
qa.a: Tell Papa early and honestly, as he did before, since honest reports are how the trust keeps growing 🙂.

qa.q: How might Francis feel when Samir tells him about the ten rupees?
qa.a: Probably reassured that his trust was well placed, since he thanked Samir and was not cross.

grounding: Illustrates a child trusted with his own savings box who reports a small mistake honestly.

passage: I'm Lalit, and my younger brother Chaitanya plays a team game every evening after homework. Lately he keeps mentioning a player called Blue Otter, who helps him win the hard levels. "He's so kind, Lalit," Chaitanya said last night, grinning at the screen. I asked whether Blue Otter knew where we live. "No! I just say I'm from India," he said, and he showed me the friend list on the screen. He also told Mummy the names of everyone he plays with. He looks happy. I can't tell how close he really feels to Blue Otter, but I keep an eye on it.

qa.q: What is the name of the player who helps Chaitanya win?
qa.a: The player is called Blue Otter.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya seem to feel about Blue Otter, and what can Lalit not know for sure?
qa.a: He seems happy and close to Blue Otter, but Lalit says he cannot tell how close Chaitanya really feels.

qa.q: What habits could Chaitanya keep up while enjoying his game friend?
qa.a: Keep private details to himself and keep telling Mummy who he plays with, as he does now.

qa.q: What might worry Lalit even though Chaitanya seems careful?
qa.a: That an online friend can still be a stranger, which is why he keeps an eye on it even though Chaitanya shows him the friend list.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling close to a kind online game player while keeping details private and telling parents who he plays with.

passage: Friday. During the match today somebody shouted insults at me on voice chat. My face went hot, my hands shook on the controller and I typed half a nasty reply 😠. Then I deleted it. I muted him and blocked him. Damini, my sister, was sitting next to me and said, "Show Mama." I didn't want to, but I did. Mama said she was sorry that happened and that I handled it well by not answering him. My chest is still a bit tight. I think the match was ruined, but I'm okay. - Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir do to the player who shouted at him?
qa.a: He muted him and blocked him.

qa.q: What did Tanvir want to do when he was shouted at?
qa.a: He wanted to hit back: his face went hot, his hands shook and he typed half a nasty reply before deleting it.

qa.q: Why is muting and blocking wiser than trading insults?
qa.a: Insults would only feed the shouting, while muting and blocking end it and telling Mama brings support.

qa.q: How might Damini have seen the moment beside Tanvir?
qa.a: She was probably worried for him and wanted him to get help, which is why she told him to show Mama.

grounding: Illustrates a child insulted in an online game who feels the urge to hit back but mutes, blocks and tells a parent.

passage: Saturday. A player called Gem_King messaged me in the game. He said he'd give me five hundred free gems if I told him my password and where I live so he could send them. My heart jumped. It felt like a lucky day. Then my cousin Pooja looked over my shoulder. "Free gems for your address? That's a warning sign." I didn't reply. I blocked him. Then I went and told Mummy, and she said I did the right thing and would report the player. My hands are still a bit buzzy. - Irfan

qa.q: What did Gem_King ask Irfan for?
qa.a: He asked for his password and where he lives.

qa.q: Why did the offer feel lucky to Irfan at first, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: Free gems felt like a lucky day and made his heart jump; then Pooja pointed out that asking for his address is a warning sign.

qa.q: What should a child do when a player asks for a password or address?
qa.a: Refuse, block the player and tell a trusted adult right away, as Irfan did.

qa.q: How does Pooja see the offer of free gems?
qa.a: As a warning sign: someone giving free things in exchange for private details is not being generous.

grounding: Illustrates a child offered free gems in return for a password and address who refuses and tells an adult.

passage: I'm Akash. Jahnavi and I have fought over the same rank in our racing game for two weeks, and it is thrilling. On Sunday she passed me on the last lap. I flung the controller onto the sofa and said nothing for ten minutes. She asked, "Are you mad?" I said no, but my ears were burning. So I switched off and went to the kitchen to bring us both water. Sitting on the balcony, I thought, she matters more than a number on a screen. When we sat down again, she grinned. "Rematch tomorrow?"

qa.q: What kind of game do Akash and Jahnavi compete in?
qa.a: They compete in a racing game.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he flung the controller onto the sofa?
qa.a: Sore pride and anger at losing, which his silence and burning ears show, although he told Jahnavi he wasn't mad.

qa.q: What could Akash do when he cannot stand losing?
qa.a: Take a break, as he did by fetching water and sitting on the balcony, and remember that Jahnavi matters more than the score.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt during Akash's silence?
qa.a: Probably a bit worried that he was upset, and her offer of a rematch suggests she values the friendship too.

grounding: Illustrates a child in fierce game rivalry with a friend who takes a break when he cannot handle losing and remembers the friend matters more.

passage: In the Class 6 maths period, Binita's pencil drew the map of her game in the margin of the notebook instead of the sums. When the teacher said her name she jumped. She hadn't heard the question. At the bell her friend Divyansh called her to cricket, and she found herself wondering what level she could reach that evening. She had no phone in school, but her stomach twisted anyway. She didn't like how much the game had followed her into class. That evening she told her parents she wanted to think about it less, and together they agreed on a fixed hour after homework and cricket on Saturdays.

qa.q: What did Binita draw in the margin of her notebook?
qa.a: She drew the map of her game.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she noticed the game had followed her into class?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit restless: her stomach twisted, and she did not like how much the game was on her mind.

qa.q: What could Binita and her parents do to keep the game in balance?
qa.a: Agree on time limits, as they did with a fixed hour after homework, and keep outdoor play like cricket in the week.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have seen Binita at the bell?
qa.a: As a friend who was distracted and far away, which may be why Divyansh called her to play cricket.

grounding: Illustrates a child who cannot stop thinking about a game in school and agrees a time limit with parents.

passage:
"Switch off now, Ujjwal."
"Papa, I'm at the key part!"
"It's been an hour."
"Five more minutes! You always ruin everything!"
Kishore folded his arms and waited. Ujjwal's face burned. He heard his own voice and winced.
"Sorry, Papa. I hate being stopped in the middle."
"I know. Tomorrow, tell me before you start, and we'll agree you finish the round."
The next evening: "One round, Papa."
"One round."
When it ended, Ujjwal switched off by himself. Kishore ruffled his hair.

qa.q: How long had Ujjwal been playing when his father asked him to stop?
qa.a: It had been an hour.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal shout at his father?
qa.a: He felt angry at being interrupted at the key part of the game, and his burning face shows the anger was strong.

qa.q: What agreement keeps the peace between Ujjwal and his father?
qa.a: Agreeing before he starts that he will finish the round and then stop, as they did the next evening 🙂.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when Ujjwal shouted?
qa.a: Probably frustrated at being shouted at, but he stayed calm and offered a plan, which suggests he cared more about a solution than about winning the moment.

grounding: Illustrates a child shouting at a parent who says switch off, and the calm agreement to finish the round then stop.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Bhavna and her cousin Kunal shared her father's old phone. A bright box popped up over the game: "Golden skin, today only!" Bhavna's thumb hovered. Her character looked plain beside the others, and a win would look good too. "Everyone will laugh at the plain one," Kunal joked. She wanted it. She also knew the game wanted her to want it. "I'll ask Papa first," she said, and went to the shed where he was mending a wheel. Papa said not today. When she came back, Kunal shrugged. "I don't care what skin you have. I like playing with you."

qa.q: Who did Bhavna go to ask before buying the golden skin?
qa.a: She went to ask Papa in the shed.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling as her thumb hovered over the golden skin?
qa.a: She was tempted: she wanted to look good and win, yet she also sensed that the game was designed to make her want it.

qa.q: Why is asking a parent before spending a wise step for Bhavna?
qa.a: The game is built to tempt, and a parent can help her decide with a cooler head and an eye on what things really cost.

qa.q: How does Kunal see the skin?
qa.a: As no big deal: he joked about it at first, but then said he did not care what skin she has and just likes playing with her.

grounding: Illustrates a child pressed by in-game purchase offers who asks a parent first and learns a friend does not care about skins.
